assessment.nobel_worthiness: GLP-1 physiology and incretin-based drugs have transformed treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity, with broad cardiometabolic benefits; a rare case of basic hormone biology translated into a global therapeutic class.
assessment.attribution: Drucker (GLP-1 biology and action), Holst (incretin physiology and GLP-1 secretion/metabolism) and Knudsen (development of long-acting liraglutide/semaglutide) span physiology to therapy. Mojsov's and others' contributions to peptide identification are contested and cannot fit a three-person prize; the allocation is a real difficulty.
assessment.maturity: Mature: multiple large, independent outcome trials and widespread clinical use confirm efficacy, and the field is highly timely.
uncertainties: Credit for the original GLP-1 sequence/activity discovery is disputed and may exclude deserving people (Mojsov, and others not on this list).
Whether the prize should reward physiology, drug design, or both is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Engineered T cells directed by chimeric antigen receptors have produced durable remissions in refractory B-cell malignancies and opened a new therapeutic modality for cancer.
assessment.attribution: Sadelain (costimulatory CAR design), June (clinical translation of CD19 CAR-T, tisagenlecleucel) and Rosenberg (adoptive cell transfer and early CAR clinical work) form a plausible trio; other early CAR pioneers (e.g. Eshhar) are not on the credited list and my recollection of their role is imperfect.
assessment.maturity: Several approved products with multi-year follow-up; clinical impact well established, though toxicity and solid-tumor limits remain.
uncertainties: Early CAR inventors outside the credited names may deserve recognition.
Rosenberg's contribution is more adoptive cell therapy broadly than CAR specifically.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Identification of BCL11A as the repressor of fetal hemoglobin from human genetics through mechanism to an approved gene-editing therapy for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia is a clean arc from genetic association to cure, with regulatory-genomics insight that fits my own area of interest.
assessment.attribution: Sankaran and Orkin defined BCL11A's role; Bauer and Orkin developed enhancer-targeted editing; Thein's GWAS/clinical genetics work is also relevant. A three-person set is feasible but not unambiguous.
assessment.maturity: Casgevy approval and clinical results are recent; long-term durability and safety data are still accruing, so timing may be slightly early.
uncertainties: Long-term durability and off-target effects of editing are not fully known.
The relative weight of the regulatory-genetics discovery versus the CRISPR editing tool (which has its own prize) is unsettled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optogenetics enabled causal, cell-type-specific control of neural activity and is now a foundational method in neuroscience, with emerging translational applications such as vision restoration.
assessment.attribution: Channelrhodopsin discovery (Nagel, Hegemann, with Bamberg) and its neuronal deployment (Deisseroth, Boyden) and Miesenboeck's earlier genetically targeted approach make credit highly crowded; any three-person set leaves out important contributors.
assessment.maturity: Method adopted across the field for two decades; independent confirmation is overwhelming, though clinical impact is still early.
uncertainties: Six or more credible contributors cannot fit into three places.
Impact is mainly as a research tool, with limited therapeutic maturity.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Discovery of cGAS-STING as the cytosolic DNA-sensing pathway revealed a basic mechanism of innate immunity with implications for infection, autoimmunity, interferonopathies and cancer immunotherapy.
assessment.attribution: Chen identified cGAS and the cyclic dinucleotide second messenger cGAMP; Barber identified STING. Two names give a coherent configuration; Ishikawa and others contributed to STING characterisation and Sun/Wu were in Chen's lab.
assessment.maturity: Mechanism is well confirmed and widely replicated; therapeutic translation (STING agonists/antagonists) is not yet proven, so the prize case rests on the basic discovery.
uncertainties: Clinical validation is limited so far.
Contributions of other STING co-discoverers may be argued as equal.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides for SMN2 gave nusinersen, a transformative therapy for spinal muscular atrophy that demonstrates the therapeutic power of RNA-processing control.
assessment.attribution: Krainer defined the SMN2 exon 7 splicing mechanism and the ASO strategy; Bennett led Ionis development of the drug. This is a compact and fair two-person set.
assessment.maturity: Approved since 2016 with long-term clinical follow-up; strong confirmation, and the concept now extends to other splicing-targeted drugs.
uncertainties: Other contributors (e.g. in the Ionis/Biogen development and earlier splice-switching work) are not credited here.
Whether the committee views this as discovery or primarily drug development is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Massively parallel sequencing-by-synthesis has reshaped biology and medicine, enabling genomics, transcriptomics including single-cell methods, cancer genomics and clinical diagnostics; its importance is difficult to overstate.
assessment.attribution: Balasubramanian and Klenerman originated the Solexa chemistry; Mayer co-developed the single-molecule array concept. Other platform inventors (Church, Rothberg, Ronaghi and others) are not on this list, and my knowledge of the precise credit division is imperfect. As a user of these methods I would be careful to avoid overweighting familiarity.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature with universal adoption, but the prize fit is uncertain because it is a technology with chemistry/technology flavour and has been recognised in adjacent contexts.
uncertainties: Fit with the Physiology or Medicine mandate and prior recognition of sequencing methods.
Platform credit is spread beyond the listed names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: TOR/mTOR was identified as a central regulator of cell growth and metabolism with major implications for cancer, ageing and immunosuppression; the discovery is original and conceptually unifying.
assessment.attribution: Hall identified TOR genetically and defined its role in growth control; Schreiber's work on the rapamycin-FKBP12 target is foundational. Sabatini and others contributed mTOR biochemistry but his inclusion is complicated; several other pioneers (e.g. Heitman, Brown, Sabatini) make allocation uncertain.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed over three decades with clinical rapalogs, though clinical efficacy beyond transplantation and a few cancers is moderate.
uncertainties: Complex and contested credit across yeast, rapamycin chemical biology and mammalian mTOR work.
Clinical impact is narrower than the biological significance.
